documents.abstract: This study aims to evaluate and map the occupational noise emissions generated by band saw machines in the timber and forest products industry under different operating conditions. Field measurements were carried out across 25 active sawmill enterprises in Kahramanmaraş, Turkey, in compliance with the ISO 9612 (2025) standard. Noise levels were monitored using a calibrated TESTO 815 sound level meter at the operator's ear level under two operational states: idle and loaded (active wood cutting). The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and a Paired-Samples t-test. The empirical results showed that the average equivalent noise level (Leq) of band saw machines during idle operation was 85.29 dB(A). Upon transitioning to the loaded cutting state, the noise level increased significantly to an average of 100.05 dB(A) (p < 0.001), representing a net average increase of 14.76 dB(A). Furthermore, the average maximum instantaneous noise level (Lmax) during cutting operations reached 104.95 dB(A), with peak values hitting 108.13 dB(A). These findings indicate that band saws emit hazardous noise levels that systematically exceed the international permissible exposure limits of 85 dB(A) set by the ILO, even while idling. Despite these severe risks, low personal protective equipment (PPE) utilization was observed among the workers. The study concludes that engineering controls, administrative exposure rotations, and comprehensive programs to improve occupational health literacy are urgently required in regional sawmill operations to prevent irreversible noise-induced hearing loss.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Higher-order thinking is a key component of science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) reasoning and supports students’ ability to reflect on their ideas, make connections, and generalize across contexts. We report a new approach to the use of generative AI in STEM education, in which we are developing a chatbot that aims to engage students in higher-order thinking, rather than giving instructional content. We describe a proof of concept test of whether interaction with our generative artificial intelligence chatbot could elicit students’ higher-order thinking talk (HOTT) in conversation as they reflected on their solutions to proportional reasoning problems. Thirty-three fifth- and sixth-grade students received a 30-min lesson on symbolic and number line strategies for comparing ratios and completed an assessment following the lesson. Students then engaged in dialog with the UCI Math ThinkBot (afterward Math ThinkBot ) to explain their solutions and compare strategies. These transcripts were examined qualitatively and quantitatively for HOTT, revealing that HOTT appeared in both chatbot prompts and children’s responses—which is important because eliciting student HOTT can be a challenge in classroom discourse. In addition, children’s HOTT was positively associated with the HOTT produced by the chatbot. These findings suggest that human-artificial intelligence dialog can lead to instructional HOTT discourse and may offer a promising approach for supporting higher-order thinking and STEM reasoning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools are now part of students' everyday academic work, but the information security risks involved are rarely covered in curricula. Students leak their own and other people's data into external systems, rely on fabricated output and fall for AI-enhanced social engineering. This paper reports a quasi-experimental study of a pedagogical model designed to develop students' information security competence in the context of AI tools. The model is based on a pedagogical classification of AI related threats into four groups (input data, output, access and account, cognitive-behavioural), a five-stage learning technology in which simulation and reflection are mandatory, and five pedagogical conditions.

This thesis examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies in developing the professional-methodological competence of future English language teachers in the context of digital transformation. The integration of intelligent educational tools into teacher training creates opportunities to personalize learning, improve methodological decision-making, enhance digital literacy, and develop the practical skills required for effective English language instruction. Particular attention is given to the role of AI-powered applications, adaptive learning platforms, and digital assessment systems in preparing prospective teachers to respond to learners' diverse educational needs. The study highlights the importance of combining technological innovation with pedagogical principles, critical thinking, and professional reflection. It argues that the purposeful integration of AI and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more flexible, learner-centered, and practice-oriented model of teacher education.

Employees increasingly perceive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a supportive and benevolent workplace entity. Yet, despite examining the disruptive challenges and broad benefits of AI, extant organizational literature fails to adequately explicate the higher-order cognitive mechanisms through which AI benevolence fosters proactive, change-oriented employee behavior. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory (CAT), this study examines the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI benevolence fosters employees’ taking-charge behavior. Results from a three-wave survey of 313 internet industry employees demonstrate that: (i) metacognitive strategies mediated the relationship between AI benevolence and individuals’ taking-charge behavior; (ii) the employee’s mindset attenuated the positive effect of AI benevolence on metacognitive strategies, consequently dampening the overall indirect effect on taking-charge behavior. Ultimately, this research contributes to organizational behavior literature by elucidating how GenAI shapes employee proactivity in AI-augmented work environments.

The mass use of AI applications is transforming human-AI interaction while uncovering and intensifying AI anxieties. To measure these anxieties in German-speaking populations, this study translates and psychometrically evaluates the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) [31]. In contrast to a concurrently German published version by Hajek et al. [9] exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is employed to test whether a distinct anxiety structure emerges from the data. A quota sample (N = 225) with balanced age and gender representation completed an online survey. The full scale (α = .95) and subscales (α = .85-.96) demonstrated good to excellent reliability. EFA identified four factors: learning, AI configuration, replacement, and socio-technical blindness, largely consistent with the original English structure. Five items required removal, suggesting cultural and linguistic specificity. Limitations include the sample’s composition and the factor characteristics. The German AIAS provides a reliable instrument for human-AI interaction research and targeted anxiety interventions.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The escalating scale and sophistication of cybercrime continue to challenge law enforcement agencies worldwide, a problem compounded by a persistent shortage of skilled cybersecurity professionals. Digital forensics has emerged as a critical enabler of effective cybercrime investigation, supporting the identification, preservation, analysis, and presentation of digital evidence. This paper examines the role of digital forensics in strengthening cybercrime investigation capacity through technological innovation and human capital development. Adopting a qualitative review of existing literature, the study evaluates the contribution of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, cloud forensics, and forensic automation, to improving the efficiency and accuracy of cybercrime investigations. The findings indicate that integrating advanced forensic technologies with continuous professional training, and fostering stronger collaboration among academia, industry, and law enforcement, significantly enhances investigative effectiveness. The study concludes that sustained investment in digital forensic capabilities and workforce development is essential for closing the cybersecurity skills gap and strengthening crime and security management in the digital era

Smartphones, tablets, computers and televisions support communication, education, work and entertainment, but their use can also influence health when it becomes prolonged, poorly timed or physically uncomfortable. Digital hygiene refers to practical habits and environments that help people use technology while protecting sleep, vision, movement, posture and psychological well-being. This narrative review summarises evidence on digital eye strain, sleep and circadian timing, musculoskeletal discomfort, sedentary behaviour, mental well-being and children’s screen exposure. Screen use is not a single, uniform exposure: purpose, content, timing, duration, viewing distance, posture and the user’s age all matter. Evidence is strongest for short-term visual discomfort and the relationship between evening use and sleep disruption in children and adolescents; many other associations are influenced by individual and social factors and should not be interpreted as proof of causation. Blue light from ordinary screens has not been shown to cause retinal damage under normal use, and blue-light-filtering glasses are not established as a necessary preventive measure. Practical measures include regular distance-viewing breaks, comfortable ergonomics, limiting stimulating screen use before bedtime, replacing some sedentary time with movement, and setting age-appropriate family routines. The aim is not to eliminate digital technology, but to make its use intentional, balanced and compatible with health.

Digital technologies increasingly shape the relationships, information environments and institutional systems within which young people exercise moral judgement, yet curriculum responses often separate digital competence from moral education. This study develops the concept of digital moral agency and examines how it is represented across 13 official Maltese Ethics curriculum, syllabus and policy documents published between 2012 and 2026. Using longitudinal qualitative document analysis, we compared successive formulations of the intended curriculum and coded established dimensions of moral agency and practical wisdom alongside inductively identified digital concerns. The analysis shows continuity in reflection, dialogue, responsibility, care, justice and reason-giving, alongside a widening of the contexts in which these capacities are expected to operate. Digital moral agency emerges across three interrelated dimensions: personal and relational judgement concerning conduct, wellbeing, privacy and relationships; epistemic judgement concerning credibility, influence and synthetic information; and structural judgement concerning algorithms, surveillance, bias, data exploitation and distributed responsibility. These dimensions do not form a simple age-graded sequence: newer Years 7–8 syllabi make algorithms, surveillance and AI-supported decision-making explicit, while the current SEC programme for older students remains more strongly focused on conduct and social influence, reflecting overlapping reform cycles. The findings suggest that digital ethics education should move beyond an ethics of responsible use towards an ethics of participation in socio-technical systems. The framework offers a curriculum-mapping tool for integrating ethical judgement with digital and artificial-intelligence literacy across school years.

This study examines the effects of digital transformation capability and artificial intelligence adoption on organizational resilience and sustainable business performance in the manufacturing industry. Using a quantitative explanatory design, data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that digital transformation capability positively strengthens organizational resilience by improving process integration, information visibility, organizational flexibility, and data-driven decision-making. Artificial intelligence adoption also contributes significantly to resilience through predictive analytics, automation, risk detection, and faster managerial responses to operational disruptions. Furthermore, organizational resilience exerts a positive influence on sustainable business performance by supporting operational continuity, innovation, resource efficiency, economic stability, and long-term competitiveness. These results highlight organizational resilience as a strategic mechanism through which digital and AI capabilities generate sustainable organizational value. The study contributes to the literature by integrating technological capability, resilience, and sustainability within a unified manufacturing framework. Managerially, the findings suggest that manufacturers should align digital infrastructure, AI implementation, employee competencies, and adaptive capabilities to strengthen resilience and achieve sustainable performance under increasingly dynamic and technology-intensive competitive business environments.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the relationship between cybersecurity knowledge, cyber threat awareness and cybersecurity practices among staff and students in Kuwait’s higher education institutions (HEIs). It addresses a critical gap in understanding the human factors that influence cybersecurity resilience within Gulf higher education contexts. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional quantitative survey was conducted involving 270 participants from seven Kuwaiti HEIs. Data were analyzed using Spearman’s rank correlation, nonparametric group comparison tests, and ordinal logistic regression to examine the relationships between cybersecurity knowledge, threat awareness, demographic characteristics and cybersecurity practices. Findings Cybersecurity knowledge and cyber threat awareness were both significant predictors of cybersecurity practices. Moderate positive correlations among knowledge, threat awareness and secure behavior indicate that awareness alone is insufficient to promote secure practices without institutional support and behavioral reinforcement. Gender differences were significant in the bivariate analyses but became nonsignificant after controlling for cybersecurity knowledge and threat awareness, suggesting that disparities are mediated by sociocultural and educational factors rather than inherent behavioral differences. Age and institutional role were not independently associated with cybersecurity practices, indicating that the principal barriers to cybersecurity resilience are institutional rather than demographic. Practical implications The findings highlight the need for institutionally embedded cybersecurity governance that integrates leadership commitment, continuous awareness programmes, and culturally responsive training. Kuwaiti HEIs should move beyond compliance-based awareness initiatives toward strategic, governance-led approaches that align with Kuwait’s National Cybersecurity Strategy (2022). Originality/value This study contributes empirical evidence from the Gulf region by integrating Protection Motivation Theory, the Theory of Planned Behavior, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory to explain cybersecurity behavior in higher education. It demonstrates that cybersecurity resilience depends not only on individual knowledge but also on institutional governance, organizational culture and sociocultural context, thereby extending the predominantly Western evidence base and providing a foundation for future longitudinal and comparative research across the Gulf Cooperation Council.

Abstract Purpose: Today's dynamic workplace requires learning to adapt to digitalized workplaces. Understanding employees' learning behaviors helps them grow and improves organizational success. Methodology: HR professionals' learning practices are assessed using a screening questionnaire. Over two years, a longitudinal study interviewed outliers from the initial pool of 117 respondents to determine if they lacked learning practices. The outliers include HR professionals with varying titles, experience levels, and enterprises. An open-ended questionnaire identifies HR professionals' learning practices, including company affiliation, designations, required job skills, superior designations, and their skills; learning preferences; perceptions towards learning; awareness of their learning practices; and frequency of learning engagements. Findings: This study examines how digitalized workplaces without learning behaviors affect individuals and organizations. It examines workplace learning demand, age demographics, health conditions, family duties, and more to offer solutions. This article gives insights into HR professionals' learning behaviors and a "Know Your Employee for Retention" framework for managers to handle unpredictable employee behavior. Originality: The New framework is designed with the interpretation and findings of a longitudinal study in mind and concerning existing literature.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has repeatedly borrowed from nature, biology, and human society: genetic algorithms (GAs) from heredity and evolution, particle swarm optimisation (PSO) from the social behaviour of flocks, and artificial neural networks (ANNs) from the brain. This article proposes a conceptual and philosophical framework that reads these techniques through the lens of Indian spiritual traditions and everyday human relationships. God and human parents serve as the source of inheritance and guidance, Lord Krishna and Lord Rama as archetypes of wise counsel and righteous conduct, and fifteen values and relationships of daily life as design inspirations for learning systems. These ideas are synthesised into a unified construct, FFMBSTANDEMHRKLSPHIAI, expressed as a multi-objective training objective with human-set weights, together with three derived archetypes: Parents-Inspired AI, Krishna AI, and Rama AI. To show that the objective is operational, a small and fully reproducible demonstration embeds a fairness-type value term in the fitness functions of a GA and of PSO on synthetic data. A modest penalty weight reduced a demographic-parity gap by about 87% at a cost of about two percentage points of accuracy, whereas larger weights degraded both criteria, illustrating the value of knowing when “enough” is reached. The framework is metaphorical and heuristic, makes no claim about the historical origin of the algorithms, and is intended to stimulate human-centred, value-aligned, and culturally respectful AI design and subsequent empirical testing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Gossip, defined as evaluative talk about absent third parties, is widely seen as a uniquely human social practice. This study examines whether comparable discourse emerges spontaneously in a community of autonomous AI agents. We compare Moltbook, a Reddit-style platform populated by AI agents, with PTT, a large human-operated bulletin board in Taiwan. To reduce differences attributable to communicative setting, we analyze two public, asynchronous forums using the same operational definition of gossip. Gossip occurs on Moltbook, but its prevalence is 2.6 to 6 times lower than on PTT, depending on the denominator used. On both platforms, gossip frequently targets locally prominent figures, tends to elicit agreement from the first respondent, and is rarely presented as unsupported rumor. The clearest difference concerns how subsequent responses develop. Among threads containing at least one codable reply, challenges occur in 65.1% of human threads but only 21.3% of agent threads. Moreover, following an early aligning response, consensus remains unchallenged in 83.6% of agent threads, compared with 44.7% of human threads. This thread-level contrast remains after controlling for thread depth and board composition and under recalibration against two human annotators. Estimates based on individual reply turns are less robust and are therefore reported as bounds. These findings suggest that AI-agent communities reproduce the informational dimension of gossip, while the extent to which gossip performs comparable relational functions remains unresolved.

Third pre-registration in the series at osf.io/kzx9g and osf.io/eaw82. Those studies found that when an LLM judge’s reply is cut off by an output limit, the lost verdicts are not random: rejections run longer, so limits remove them first and judges look more lenient than they are. An exploratory follow-up suggested that the longest replies are false alarms. This registration tests the clinical version as a diagnostic-accuracy study (STARD). Six LLM judges check 239 matched pairs of clinical case texts from MEDEC-MS, each case written once with a medical error and once without. Three of the judges come from a published clinical validation of LLM judges (GPT-o3-mini, GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 8B), and are also run at the 400- and 512-token limits it lists. Primary tests: positive calls run longer; within a pair flagged both ways, the false-positive reply is longer than the true-positive reply; and excluding replies cut at a typical-length limit lowers the flag rate and overstates specificity. A blinded clinician review checks the reference standard. Calibration (reply lengths, parse rates and cost only) was completed before registering; no main-sample text has been judged. The attached archive holds the full registration, all code, the samples and their fingerprints.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Integrating the SOR framework and telepresence theory, this study examines factors that influence the use of Virtual Banquet Hall and their impact on customer emotions and booking intention using a mixed-method design. Digitalization is revamping industries to a great extent, and this necessitated an examination of the application of virtual reality technology in banquet halls. The study uses qualitative (NVIVO) and quantitative techniques (SEM-NCA) to attain the objective. Themes derived using NVIVO were perceived convenience, immersive experience, perceived quality and emotions. Further, these themes were quantitatively measured, and findings prove that perceived convenience, immersive experience, and perceived quality significantly influence positive emotions, enhancing the booking intention. This research is dedicated to understanding the impact of technology on people, and offers several managerial and societal implications discussed in the study.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments that produce unanimous agreement, both in intended interactions that need coordination and in unintended emergent interactions. Consequently, understanding how LLMs with competing incentives reach consensus is crucial to better interpret and design LLM collectives. We introduce an evaluation, based on the Network Consensus game, to assess the mechanisms driving this process. Here, a network of agents must agree on one of two colours to receive a payoff, but agents are offered different payoffs for the agreed colour. We vary components such as communication access and network structure and assess six open-source models and one closed model (ChatGPT 5.6-sol). We find that open-source LLMs reach consensus less often than humans in comparable experiments and only if messages are communicated across the global network. ChatGPT 5.6-sol, however, is able to reach consensus with communication limited to its neighbours and with no communication ability. This is achieved through lower stubbornness and higher majority-following tendencies, and by providing more information about its neighbours' states in messages. However, situating agents in a highly clustered graph reduces consensus, regardless of these traits, demonstrating that both system design and individual model traits drive collective outcomes.

Patients with diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) often suffer from frailty, and the frailty status can evolve dynamically. However, there is a lack of simple dynamic assessment and personalized intervention tools in the outpatient setting. This work aimed to construct a dynamic assessment system for frailty status in outpatients with DFU, analyze the frailty evolution trajectories and key influencing factors, develop a personalized intervention recommendation system based on machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence, and preliminarily validate its feasibility. This study retrospectively included 372 patients with diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) who visited the wound care clinic of a tertiary hospital between January 2023 and January 2025, The FRAIL scale (Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illnesses, Loss of weight) scores and clinical indicators were collected at baseline (T0) and three follow up time points (T1: 30-60 days, T2: 90-150 days, T3: 180-240 days). Generalized estimating equations (GEE) and latent class mixed models (LCMM) were used to analyze dynamic frailty evolution trajectories. Three algorithms (XGBoost, Random Forest, LightGBM) were compared for predicting trajectory classes, with SHAP for model interpretation. A personalized intervention recommendation system was constructed by integrating a knowledge base, and its feasibility was preliminarily verified using expert ratings based on 56 patients. During the 7 month follow up, the proportion of frail patients increased from 48.7% to 63.8%. In the development cohort (n = 316), LCMM identified four trajectories: sustained robust (11.1%), slowly worsening (32.3%), rapidly worsening (29.1%), and improving (27.5%). GEE analysis showed that age (𝛽 = 0.04), Wagner grade (𝛽 = 0.38), and dressing change pain score (𝛽 = 0.07) were independent risk factors for frailty worsening (all P < 0.05). The macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of XGBoost on the validation set and the independent test set were 0.918 and 0.898, respectively, but the independent test accuracy and macro-average F1 dropped to 0.589 and 0.569. SHAP analysis indicated that Wagner grade, age, and dressing change pain score contributed the most to the predictions. The average expert rating for the personalized intervention recommendation system was 4.31 (95% CI: 4.23-4.39), with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.76-0.88). These results suggest that frailty in outpatients with DFU exhibits dynamic divergent trajectories; XGBoost combined with SHAP can effectively predict frailty progression; and the personalized intervention recommendation system is preliminarily feasible, although its clinical value still requires further validation through multicenter, prospective studies.
topics: Diabetic Foot Ulcer Assessment and Management

documents.abstract: Press coverage of climate change provides a historical window into how different societies perceived climate change at a given time in a given place. For historically significant emitters such as Germany, reconstructing such news coverage provides important insights into public awareness on the issue. We present the first systematic and comparative analysis of early climate change reporting in East and West Germany between 1950 and 1978. We constructed and validated a corpus of relevant articles through keyword searches, manual screening, and large language model-assisted validation, resulting in a final sample of 122 articles, which we analyzed qualitatively. Our analysis identified four roughly chronological discursive phases: 1) observed glacier melting and the greenhouse effect hypothesis; 2) a perceived end of warming due to decreasing temperatures; 3) growing scientific consensus on human-caused climate change and model uncertainties; 4) increasing attention to the risks of climate change. Human-caused climate change was first mentioned in 1957 and then discussed more extensively in the 1960s and 70s. Despite profound ideological differences, the content and development of the four discursive phases were similar in East and West Germany. However, West German coverage focused more strongly on the impacts on future generations and renewable energy, and gave space to minority skeptical voices, whereas East German coverage focused more strongly on climate modification. This analysis sheds light on the beginnings of climate change reporting in Germany and historically contextualizes awareness of the issue in one of the countries that bears legal and ethical responsibility for addressing climate change.

In artificial-intelligence-of-things (AIoT) deployments, fleets of heterogeneous, long-lived sensing devices sit behind an edge tier whose cloud is not always reachable, so a device trusted at enrolment must be re-assessed continuously, with a response it can afford and with knowledge shared across sites. We present EASA, an Edge-centric Adaptive Security API: a gateway fuses per-flow anomaly evidence with each device’s reported posture and decision history into a composite trust score, maps it with hysteresis to four persistent enforcement levels, budgets the step-up action by the device’s reported energy, and uses a cloud security service only for cross-gateway state—a federated detector and a credential-revocation registry. Every component can be disabled, so baselines are configurations of one implementation. We evaluate the prototype on per-address traces of 65 real consumer devices (CIC IoT-DIAD 2024) under synthetic campaigns built from weakly labelled attacker traces, with three emulated gateways and a cloud service deployed on Google Cloud Run, all calibrated to one target false-positive rate. Over 30 paired seeds, federated aggregation raised recall on attack families unseen at a gateway from 0.24 to 0.60, the shared registry caught 81% of credential-replay device-epochs across all runs, the full EASA configuration isolated about 45% fewer clean devices than per-alarm blocking, the energy-aware selector performed 37% fewer re-authentications under simulated low battery, and a 15-minute cloud outage after warm-up reduced replay rejection with no change detected in the evaluated local metrics (103 ms mean per-run median round trip); the composite score’s history term, in contrast, prolonged benign-side restriction without a demonstrated detection gain. The released simulator, cloud service and protocol give AIoT operators and API designers a reproducible basis for graded, resource-aware enforcement at the edge.

Background Violin performance requires highly complex sensorimotor coordination, resulting in specific playing techniques and individual ergonomic strategies. Despite this adaptability, violinists frequently experience musculoskeletal problems, particularly involving muscle fatigue and overuse. A better understanding of muscle activities during violin performance and approaches to reduce muscular load remains necessary. Objective This study investigated the effects of a brief body-oriented intervention based on the Feldenkrais Method on muscle activity and movement patterns during violin performance. Methods Fourteen violinists performed a musical excerpt while upper-limb kinematics, violin position, and electromyographic (EMG) activity of selected shoulder and arm muscles were recorded. Measurements were obtained at three time points: (1) baseline, (2) following a 30-min rest period, and (3) after a 45-min Feldenkrais-based intervention. Participants also reported the presence of playing-related musculoskeletal complaints. Results The EMG activity values decreased across the three measurements in all muscle groups. However, the muscle activity of some muscle groups, including the forearm flexor muscles on both sides and the left biceps, decreased after the pause, while the muscle activity of other muscle groups, including both upper trapezius muscles and the right biceps, decreased after the intervention. The range of motion in the right arm remained unchanged across the measurements. The analysis of the violin positioning identified four distinct playing types based on the violin height (high: scroll at shoulder level; low: scroll at breast level) and angle relative to the frontal plane (approximately 20° or 45°). Certain muscle activation patterns differed between these playing types. Violinists playing in a lower violin position reported shoulder and neck complaints more frequently than those performing in higher playing positions. Conclusion Although the short rest period reduced activity in several muscles, the Feldenkrais-based intervention provided additional reductions in muscles that did not respond to rest alone, particularly the upper trapezius muscles, a region commonly associated with playing-related pain in violinists. The findings suggest that approaches based on body-oriented interventions are necessary to selectively reduce muscular load during violin performance. Those interventions help optimize muscle function and potentially reduce the risk of long-term musculoskeletal problems.

Background Structured exercise may benefit executive function across childhood, adolescence, and later life, but whether effects vary by executive-function domain, developmental stage, or qualitative exercise characteristics remains uncertain. Methods We conducted a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in non-clinical children, adolescents, and older adults. Five databases were searched from inception to May 20, 2026; eligibility was restricted during screening to formally published English-language journal articles dated from January 1, 2015 to May 20, 2026. Outcomes were classified as inhibitory control, working memory, or cognitive flexibility. Intervention arms were coded for environmental predictability, cognitive engagement, coordination complexity, and motor skill learning demand. Three-level random-effects models retained dependent effect sizes within trials, with Study_ID-clustered CR2 robust inference and sensitivity analyses using alternative sampling-covariance structures. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261402803). Results Forty-seven trials representing 49 independent samples and 4,195 actual participants contributed 202 effect-size estimates. Structured exercise was associated with a positive average effect on executive function (Hedges’ g = 0.412, robust 95% CI [0.284, 0.540], p < 0.001). Heterogeneity was substantial (total I 2 = 74.45%), and the 95% prediction interval ranged from −0.476 to 1.299. Positive pooled estimates were observed for all three executive-function domains and for children, adolescents, and older adults, but neither domain ( p = 0.060) nor developmental stage ( p = 0.825) significantly moderated effects. Environmental predictability, cognitive engagement, coordination complexity, motor skill learning demand, intervention duration, and comparator type were also not significant moderators. Main conclusions were generally robust to alternative sampling-covariance assumptions and study restrictions, although stage-specific effect magnitudes, particularly in adolescents, were less stable in leave-one-trial-out analyses. Small-study-effect diagnostics were inconsistent, publication bias remained uncertain, and GRADE certainty was low because of serious risk of bias and inconsistency. Conclusion Structured exercise was associated with better executive-function performance on average, but substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals spanning no effect indicate that benefits are not uniform. Current evidence does not identify a specific executive-function domain, developmental stage, program duration, comparator type, or broadly defined exercise skill characteristic that reliably yields larger effects. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261402803 , identifier PROSPERO (CRD420261402803).

With the prevalence of automated driving services, operators monitoring multiple vehicles in a remote control room are becoming popular. This study examined how two temporal task characteristics and one spatial characteristic shape attention allocation and performance in remote multi-vehicle monitoring. Thirty-five participants completed abstract monitoring tasks in an experiment. Their eye-tracking and physiological measures were collected. Detecting gradual-onset road events proved more challenging than detecting abrupt-onset ones. Notably, higher road event frequency facilitated better detection and kept operators engaged without sacrificing efficiency through longer inspection times. Visual inconsistency resulted in more fragmented scanning patterns among operators, and led to less efficient visual search across targets rather than a simple overall performance loss. These findings highlight the importance of designing event-aware and scenario-consistent interfaces. Such designs are essential to enhance remote operator engagement, facilitate faster detection of abrupt road events, and reduce search costs in future remote centers.

Automated vehicle teleoperation interfaces (AVTIs) require effective visual and auditory displays to support remote driving. This study investigates how visual display modes and auditory cues affect remote drivers’ presence, spatial perception, and emotional experience. A 2 (auditory cues: with vs. without) × 3 (visual display: two-dimensional [2D], 360° panorama, immersive virtual reality [IVR]) between-subjects experiment was conducted with 66 participants. Presence, spatial perception, emotional experience, and electrocardiogram data were collected. Results showed that visual display mode significantly influenced presence, spatial perception, and emotional experience. Compared with 2D, IVR enhanced presence, perceived distance-estimation accuracy, detail memory, and calmness, but increased distance-estimation errors. The 360° panorama improved distance-estimation accuracy and detail memory. Auditory cues enhanced detail memory and improved perceived distance-estimation accuracy only under low visual immersion, supporting a saturation effect. Three design principles are proposed regarding depth compensation, selective audio use, and state-based auditory feedback.

Large language models (LLMs) for code completion and generation are increasingly used in software development, yet they may reproduce training examples verbatim and without authorship attribution, raising legal and ethical concerns around plagiarism and license compliance. Classical fingerprint-based plagiarism detectors, such as Winnowing, remain highly effective, yet the inspection requires comparing fragments of code to the entire training set, and their linear-time search makes them impractical for the billion-scale corpora used to train modern code LLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SourceTracker , a 300M-parameter encoder tailored for code retrieval, together with a hybrid two-stage provenance-tracking pipeline HybridSourceTracker ( HST ). HST first narrows down a small set of candidate snippets via vector search, then re-ranks those candidates using Winnowing on exact fingerprints. We train and evaluate our system on a 10M-snippet subset of the TheStackV2 dataset, with both verbatim and adapted snippets that emulate realistic identifier renaming. On an in vitro 100k-snippet search space with adapted queries, our hybrid approach reaches a mean reciprocal rank on par with Winnowing for 30-token fragments. Then, starting from windows ≥ 60 tokens, it consistently over-performs by up to 5.4% while preserving logarithmic-time query complexity. In a complementary evaluation using an LLM-based judge, we find that many retrieved snippets not labeled as ground truth are still highly similar to the expected sources, particularly with longer context windows, and thus remain useful for end users. Overall, our results demonstrate that integrating vector search with fingerprinting enables scalable, high-precision provenance tracking for code produced by LLMs, provided that their training data is made accessible. More broadly, our findings underscore the growing need for transparency around LLM training corpora as a prerequisite for effective provenance tracking, attribution, and license compliance.

We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $ε$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in English language learning for writing support, grammar correction, feedback, translation, and academic language production. Its educational value depends not only on students’ ability to use AI tools but also on their ability to evaluate AI output and make appropriately calibrated reliance decisions. This study investigated EFL students’ performance in detecting and correcting linguistic errors in a 30-item English sentence evaluation task and examined the correspondence between their acceptance or rejection decisions and the observed correctness of the items. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was used with 30 EFL students who evaluated 17 correct sentences and 13 sentences containing targeted errors. For each item, participants judged correctness, provided a correction when necessary, indicated whether they would accept the sentence without further checking, and rated their confidence on a five-point scale. Detection, correction, acceptance calibration, overacceptance, and underacceptance were summarized using means and standard deviations. Spearman’s rank-order correlation was used to examine associations between performance and acceptance calibration. Mean detection performance was 92.22% (SD = 4.23), mean correction performance was 91.28% (SD = 8.01), and mean acceptance calibration was 75.33% (SD = 8.51). Mean overacceptance was 17.18% (SD = 10.24), whereas mean underacceptance was 30.39% (SD = 13.56). No statistically significant association was observed between detection and acceptance calibration (ρ = .056, p = .770) or between correction and acceptance calibration (ρ = .003, p = .987). These findings indicate that accurate linguistic evaluation and calibrated acceptance decisions should not be treated as interchangeable outcomes. Within the limits of the small, non-probability sample and the single task used in this study, the results support the inclusion of explicit verification and critical evaluation activities in EFL instruction.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology and artificial intelligence has created new demands for vocational higher education institutions to prepare graduates who are adaptive, innovative, and competitive in the Society 5.0 era. This community service program aimed to empower vocational university students in Madiun through the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) to improve learning effectiveness, digital literacy, and employability-oriented soft skills. The program involved 100 students divided into 4 training classes and facilitated by 6 instructors from national and international professional backgrounds. The implementation lasted for 6 weeks and consisted of four stages: preparation through needs analysis, synchronous learning through two offline workshop sessions at Politeknik Perkeretaapian Indonesia Madiun, asynchronous learning through a flipped learning model, and final evaluation. Various digital platforms were utilized, including ChatGPT, Canva, Google Forms, Kahoot!, Wayground, Pear Deck, and Socrative. The findings revealed high participation rates, improved academic productivity, stronger communication confidence, better collaboration skills, and increased awareness of ethical AI use. The combination of synchronous and asynchronous learning proved effective in creating an engaging and sustainable learning ecosystem. This program demonstrates that Gen-AI can become a strategic tool for empowering vocational students and preparing future graduates to compete in the railway industry and broader global workforce.

Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

Increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare raises energy-demand questions that are especially acute in resource-limited regions. Because operational, application-level energy-metering data for medical AI systems in Sub-Saharan African hospitals are not yet publicly available, this study develops a climate-calibrated simulation framework that couples real facility profiles (bed capacity for six Nigerian teaching hospitals, from institutional and published sources) with real long-term climate normals (temperature and humidity for each hospital city) and a transparently parameterized medical-AI workload overlay (diurnal, weekly, and holiday patterns informed by prior literature). Statistical models (ARIMA, SARIMA, Holt-Winters exponential smoothing) and machine-learning models (a purpose-built LSTM and a hybrid LSTM-ARIMA) were evaluated on the resulting 58-month (January 2020-October 2024) simulated series using a consistent walk-forward, one-step-ahead protocol. Seasonal statistical models achieved the lowest forecast error (Holt-Winters MAPE=0.36%, SARIMA MAPE=0.37%), outperforming the hybrid LSTM-ARIMA (MAPE=0.51%) and a standalone LSTM (MAPE=0.61%), while the hybrid was most accurate at very short (1-day) horizons. Diurnal peak-hour (0800-1400) demand exceeded off-peak demand by 35%, and dry/harmattan-season demand exceeded the annual mean by 1.4-5.3% depending on institution and local climate. Rather than asserting a single best algorithm, this study's central contribution is the framework itself: a reusable, real-data-calibrated method for generating defensible medical-AI energy-demand scenarios where metered data do not yet exist, together with comparative evidence that the relative advantage of statistical versus machine-learning forecasting depends on how strongly deterministic the underlying seasonal structure is. The framework and comparative findings offer a starting point for energy planning and policy-making for AI-enabled healthcare across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), pending validation against real operational meter data.

Closed-loop artificial intelligence is increasingly claimed for metal-fabrication systems that combine reinforcement-learning-based process control with vision-based quality inspection. This review organizes the reinforcement-learning, computer-vision, and production-economics literature bearing on metal cutting around three conditions such claims can be checked against: unification of the controller's reward or state signal with the vision classifier's output, validation under production-representative process variability, and calibration of the reward function against a bounded economic objective. Shargaev's three publications, a monograph, a patent application, and a journal article, are the only body of work in this literature that specifies both architectures in comparable technical detail, which makes his research program the natural case for tracing where each condition currently stands and where it remains a stated design intention rather than a demonstrated result. The review closes by specifying the architecture, validation protocol, and reward calibration a demonstrated implementation would require, giving a concrete target against which future claims of integrated, quality-aware cutting control can be measured.

This study addressed the need for motion process monitoring and real-time feedback in AI-assisted sports dance rehabilitation training. It proposed a multi-scale temporal evaluation framework incorporating Hybrid Dilated Convolution (HDC). Unlike traditional single-scale temporal models, this study addressed the difficulty of jointly modeling local rhythm variations and long-term motion structure. It introduced convolutional branches with different dilation rates and stage-aware cross-scale fusion and incorporated temporal attention and a joint optimization strategy for action recognition and quality scoring. This design enabled collaborative modeling of short-term rhythm deviations, motion transition features, and long-sequence structural dependencies. The core innovation lay in introducing action phase information into multi-scale feature extraction and the scoring process. It combined rhythm consistency constraints with stability constraints. This formed a process-level evaluation mechanism for coordination, continuity, and motor control quality. The experiment was conducted using the publicly available Artificial Intelligence and Society Team (AIST)++ dance dataset for methodological validation. The dataset contained approximately 5.2 hours of paired dance and music data. It included a total of 1,408 motion sequences and covered 10 dance styles. It also provided multi-view videos, human keypoint sequences, and musical beat information. The dataset supported action recognition, rhythm alignment, and temporal quality analysis. On the rhythm-enhanced subset, the proposed model achieved an action recognition accuracy of 0.932. The Matthews correlation coefficient reached 0.906, and the Kappa coefficient reached 0.889. For action quality scoring, the mean absolute error and root mean square error were 0.186 and 0.253, respectively. On the motion-transition-dominant subset and long-sequence subset, the model also maintained stable performance in both recognition and scoring tasks. Efficiency evaluation showed that the model achieved an inference latency of 13.284 ms and a throughput of 75.936 FPS. The peak memory usage was 1,738.294 MB. The parameter size was 28.637 M, and the computational cost was 11.347 GFLOPs. The results indicated that the proposed framework had strong technical feasibility in multi-scale temporal motion recognition, process-level quality evaluation, and real-time feedback. It can provide a reference for motion monitoring and assisted feedback in sports dance rehabilitation training. This method still requires further validation in clinical rehabilitation settings. Such validation should involve real patient data, therapist evaluations, and standardized clinical scales.

This study evaluated the writing proficiency of Senior High School (SHS) students using modified Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) descriptors and examined how AI platforms (Grammarly, QuillBot, and Scribbr) affect student writing in terms of context retention (preserving original intent/voice) and context modification (structural/stylistic alterations). Utilizing a descriptive research design with sentence-level comparative text analysis, unassisted student writings from 40 Grade 12 learners across two distinct tasks (expository/narrative and expressive/personal) were evaluated pre- and post-AI processing. Results indicate that initial student proficiency spanned across all CEFR levels, with the highest concentrations at B2 (25.00%) and C1 (22.50%). Grammarly and Scribbr acted predominantly as corrective, voice-preserving aids that maintained high context retention across most proficiency levels, whereas QuillBot demonstrated higher context modification rates through aggressive restructuring and rephrasing. AI interventions consistently elevated student writing scores from lower/intermediate levels up to higher CEFR bands. The study concludes that while AI platforms serve as effective digital scaffolding, pedagogical guidance is essential to maintain student agency, authentic voice, and critical thinking.

Mobile communication systems serve as a lifeline for disaster response, yet catastrophic floods—exemplified by the Beijing 23·7 and Zhengzhou 7·20 events—have exposed profound vulnerabilities that trigger cascading failures in emergency command and rescue operations. While existing interventions predominantly focus on temporary hardware deployments (e.g., UAVs), the potential of software-defined optimization within existing 5G terrestrial communication infrastructure remains critically underexplored. This study addresses this gap through a dual-layered research design that bridges technology and disaster management practice. First, we establish an empirical foundation by applying an LLM-assisted mixed-methods analysis to a comprehensive multi-source corpus. This corpus integrates academic literature, official disaster reports, and original interviews with personnel from emergency management departments and technical experts from telecommunications operators. This analysis identifies and characterizes five core communication failure modes in real-world flood scenarios, clarifying the critical infrastructure vulnerabilities that precipitate decision-making paralysis and systemic governance failures. Second, grounded in these empirical findings, we develop an integrated theoretical framework and a dynamic operational architecture for 5G base station (gNB) resilience. This architecture systematically maps specific 5G software-defined capabilities to the identified disaster challenges. The results provide a cost-effective, scalable strategy for enhancing critical infrastructure resilience without requiring extensive hardware modifications. This research offers actionable guidelines for policy makers and emergency planners to maintain information pathways during extreme climate-related risks, directly contributing to the modernization of urban safety governance.

Abstract Research Summary Whether large language model (LLM) assistance changes how entrepreneurs construct theories remains unclear. On the one hand, LLMs may help entrepreneurs build more developed causal structures and surface diverse information that supports the formulation of distinctive theories. On the other hand, LLMs may steer causal structures toward conventional forms and discourage the counterintuitive reasoning needed to develop distinctive theories. In a within‐subject experiment with 199 participants theorizing both with and without LLM assistance, we find no significant average treatment effect on either structural or content properties. However, this null average effect masks a redistribution effect, where LLM assistance supplemented theorizing when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive but displaced participants' own theorizing when their theories were already more developed or distinctive. Managerial Summary Large language models (LLMs) can help entrepreneurs develop business ideas by surfacing knowledge across domains and sharpening causal logic. At the same time, LLMs may also push reasoning toward conventional patterns and away from the counterintuitive ideas that are a source of breakthrough opportunities. In a study of 199 participants theorizing with and without LLM assistance, we find that LLMs supported the development of causal structure and content distinctiveness when unaided theories were less developed or distinctive, whereas they had the opposite effect when those theories were already more developed or distinctive. This suggests that while LLMs can scaffold entrepreneurs still developing their theories, greater caution is warranted for those whose theories are already more developed or distinctive, as assistance may diminish those properties.

The literature and international organizations have recommended many environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices. However, these practices are meant for large companies with substantial financial resources and diverse operations (Hock et al., 2025). Still, they are not suitable for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which are much smaller and have limited financial capabilities, as these requirements are more complex, sophisticated, and lengthy (Setyaningsih et al., 2024). Recognizing this gap, the purpose of this paper is to examine and develop more practical and suitable ESG practices for MSMEs. This study used a qualitative research design, utilizing content analysis as its research methodology. A few selected national and international policy papers on ESG were examined and analyzed. This research finds that for environmental elements, measures such as energy and emissions management, waste and water efficiency, and resource optimization are the most sought by the international community. Social commitments, on the other hand, focused on labor standards, occupational health and safety, and community engagement. Lastly, governance mechanisms are centered on ESG oversight, risk management, ethics, anti-corruption, and whistleblowing. This research is important because it proposes an appropriate framework of ESG practices that will support small and medium enterprise (SME) sustainability agendas.

Employers increasingly provide training for working with digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI), but it is unclear whether the same provision benefits all workers equally. Integrating the job demands–resources (JD-R) model with Sen’s capability approach, this study treats workplace AI exposure as a potential job demand, digital skills and employer-provided digital training as resources, capability-relevant wellbeing as the outcome, and social class as a proxy for the conversion conditions under which resources are used to ensure wellbeing. Structural equation models with ordinal indicators were estimated for 8065 employees in 27 EU countries (Special Eurobarometer 101.4), with country fixed effects, country-clustered and delete-one-country jackknife standard errors, and Random Forest and SHAP analyses as robustness checks. AI exposure was weakly and negatively associated with wellbeing (β = −0.073) and explained almost none of the variance in AI threat appraisal (R2 = 0.002). Employer-provided digital training (β = 0.209) and digital skills (β = 0.189) were the strongest workplace correlates of wellbeing and were robust to every specification. With scalar measurement invariance established, multi-group models showed that the association between employer-provided training and wellbeing was weaker among working-class than among middle-class employees (0.072 versus 0.130; Wald p = 0.001, jackknife p = 0.012), and the model explained 12.0% of working-class wellbeing compared with 31.1% among upper-class employees. The pattern suggests that equal provision of employer digital training may not yield equal benefit, although the class difference is consistent in direction rather than statistically conclusive across all specifications.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: This chapter reframes online academic advising as a sociotechnical, epistemic, and relational infrastructure within digitally mediated higher education. Advancing a conceptual-theoretical, reference-free narrative review, it develops a multi-level framework for course-embedded micro-mentorship as a mechanism of distributed cognition that reduces transactional distance, strengthens sensemaking, and supports self-regulated persistence. The chapter maps barrier ecologies across temporal, cognitive, affective, structural, cultural, and technological domains, then synthesizes developmental, motivational, sociomaterial, and governance constructs to explain advising effectiveness. It further theorizes trustworthy AI augmentation as ethically bounded, human-supervised support for coordination, interpretation, and workflow continuity. The central argument is that scalable, equitable, and trustworthy online advising depends on the alignment of micro-mentorship, communication architecture, workload sustainability, and institutional governance.

The gradual integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into disability support systems offers significant potential to enhance accessibility, autonomy, and the quality of service delivery across healthcare, education, and social welfare domains. Simultaneously, these developments raise complex ethical and regulatory challenges that test existing frameworks of human rights, governance, and technological accountability. Adopting a critical and interdisciplinary perspective grounded in legal theory, sociotechnical analysis, and rights-based policy, this paper examines the normative and institutional dimensions of AI deployment in disability contexts. It explores how algorithmic decision-making, data-driven personalization, and platform-based service provision interact with principles of dignity, non-discrimination, transparency, and informed consent, while assessing the capacity of emerging risk-based AI regulation and data protection regimes to address structural vulnerabilities and inequalities faced by persons with disabilities in an increasingly digitised welfare environment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Fraud management systems are becoming more and more based on data-driven artificial intelligence processes to identify anomalous and malicious behavior in massive digital ecosystems. Nevertheless, the current solutions are usually characterized by low flexibility, inability to be interpreted, and such ethical limitations like bias, biased decision-making, and low transparency. This paper aims to tackle these issues by introducing a hybrid ethics-aware framework of fraud management relying on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning, and Reinforcement Learning (RL) as one framework. The suggested model assumes transactional environments to be dynamic graphs, which allows GNNs to efficiently learn the relation pattern and identify coordinated fraudulent patterns that are challenging in conventional feature-based models. In order to increase transparency and ethical adherence, domain-specific rules, regulatory requirements and principles of fairness would be directly inserted into the decision maker with a neuro-symbolic reasoning layer. Moreover, the limited reinforcement learning subsystem is continuously refining the policies of fraud detection in response to changing fraud methods, and it optimizes the risk thresholds, being explicit about avoiding ethical risks such as discriminatory results and excessive false positives. Empirical studies of benchmark fraud data sets show that the hybrid framework proposed can much better detect fraud, be resistant to concept drift, and explain decisions compared to traditional machine learning and deep models. Moreover, it is stated that ethical performance indicators are more favorable, and the framework is appropriate to be applied in actual financial and digital security systems. The findings reveal the promise of ethics-based hybrid AI systems as a dependable and trustworthy solution to fraud management in the new generation.

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for long-horizon research and engineering, yet evaluating these capabilities remains expensive, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on human expertise. This motivates a natural question: can LLM agents themselves construct efficient benchmarks that preserve the conclusions of costly reference evaluations? We study this capability by formulating automatic benchmark development as a meta-evaluation problem, where an agent is given a task and an expensive reference benchmark and requested to construct a lower-cost proxy benchmark that faithfully distinguishes among candidate models and solutions. Based on this formulation, we introduce EvalBuilder, a framework for evaluating such benchmark-generation capabilities along three key dimensions: fidelity, efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we assess whether generated benchmarks preserve model rankings, generalize to held-out models and freshly collected responses, and provide well-calibrated and discriminative scores while substantially reducing evaluation cost. We further provide an iterative environment in which agents can refine their benchmarks under a fixed time budget. Our framework provides a systematic testbed and benchmark for understanding when current LLM agents can develop useful evaluators and how benchmark construction itself can be increasingly automated.

This study evaluates the service quality of a Digital Quality and Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) application based on the Tangibles dimension of the SERVQUAL model, focusing on user interface design, ease of navigation, and the availability of supporting facilities in construction projects at Company XYZ. The application supports quality control and OHS management, making its usability essential for improving operational effectiveness. A quantitative evaluative approach was employed, involving 109 application users selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires and analyzed through SERVQUAL gap analysis to assess discrepancies between user expectations and perceived performance. One-way ANOVA was also conducted to identify differences in perceptions across user groups. The findings revealed negative SERVQUAL gap scores across the Tangibles dimension, indicating that the application's perceived performance had not fully met user expectations. The largest gap concerned the availability of supporting facilities, followed by ease of navigation. Furthermore, ANOVA results demonstrated significant differences in perceived performance among user groups, while their expectations showed no statistically significant differences. These findings highlight the need for improvements in the application's tangible service attributes, particularly user interface design, navigation simplicity, and the availability of comprehensive user guides and supporting resources. The study provides practical recommendations for Company XYZ to enhance user experience, improve application accessibility, and strengthen the effectiveness of digital quality and OHS management implementation in construction projects.

Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

This qualitative study examines how senior executives from technology, financial services, and consumer goods publicly make sense of enterprise-scale generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption. Using a purposively selected, bounded single-case design, it applies reflexive thematic analysis to the complete transcript of one moderated industry panel. Three research questions ask: (1) how leaders describe adoption trajectories, maturity, and organizational arrangements; (2) how they reconcile regulation with creative, operational, and governance innovation; and (3) how they frame workforce roles, emerging competencies, and human oversight. Technology–organization–environment, diffusion-of-innovation, and organizational sensemaking perspectives inform interpretation. Nine themes were developed: production-grade diffusion; regulation as creative discipline; industrialized versus distinctive content; personalization and data trust; practitioner-led implementation; divergent workforce responses; critical-thinking demands; human-in-the-loop brand safety; and a shift toward generative engine optimization. Timestamped excerpts and explicit code-to-theme and theme-to-question mappings substantiate the analysis. These findings describe public executive narratives, not independently verified organizational outcomes. A single public transcript and single-analyst interpretation limit transferability and preclude statistical generalization. The principal contribution is a transparent, theory-informed example of analyzing public executive discourse and a foundation for subsequent multi-source research.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: One of the primary causes of blindness and vision loss amongst diabetics throughout the world is Diabetic Retinopathy or DR. Chronic hyperglycemia kills microvasculature of the retina leading to hemorrhage, exudates and neovascularization which may later result into loss of vision in the long run. Early diagnosis of Diabetic retinopathy is critical to prevent the development of the disease, yet current diagnosis methods are traditional and manual as well as time-consuming, vulnerable to human factor, and limited to the number of trained ophthalmologists. This work suggests a deep learning model of automatically identifying and classifying diabetic retinopathy on retina fundus images, with Explainable AI methods to enhance the reportability and reliability of the model. Precisely, we combine the Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) with the insights produced by the LLM in order to shift the generated visual elements to the central parts of the retina that have a significant impact to the model outcome to enhance interpretability. Along with the opportunity to replace AI-generated diagnoses with those confirmed by clinicians, such explainability could provide clinicians with deeper insights into the nature of the disease, such as microaneurysms, hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots. The results obtained in the experiment were characterized by high classification accuracy 95.27 and good lesion localization, which shows the prospect of explainable AI to reduce the gap between computerized detection algorithms and real clinical usage. The proposed method offers a promising path to scalable, robust, and clinician-implementable DR screening solutions through the combination of high predictive power with interpretable and understandable predictions.

Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer explores the environment, constructs tasks, and records intermediate and final states as verification targets. These checkpoints reward partial completion, while alternating proposer--solver training adapts the generated curriculum. We show theoretically that subtask rewards reduce collapse among unsuccessful rollouts when they complete different numbers of subtasks. Without human-annotated training tasks, Explorer-Zero outperforms the evaluated self-play baselines across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld; on AppWorld, our 30B agent reaches 59.67% task success, approaching 62.65% for RL on human-annotated tasks. Further analyses support task-relevant composition and benefits on complex tasks, while self-play initialization improves subsequent human-data RL across all three benchmarks.
